Next, regarding the teachings, its meaning is explained according to the twelvefold division of the scriptures as set forth in the chapter. If one relies on the original teaching, it is included within the tenfold division;

however, the *itivṛttaka* (past events) only explains the past deeds of disciples, while the *jātaka* (birth stories) speaks only of the Buddha’s past lives; therefore, [the former] is not the *itivṛttaka*.

Regarding those included within the Jātaka that rely on the provisional teachings (*neyārtha*), they are subsumed solely under the category of *śāstra* (treatises), while the remaining eleven divisions consist exclusively of the Buddha’s own words (*sūtra*).
This is because the category of *śāstra* is transmitted through the disciples, whereas the *sūtra* category is transmitted directly from the Buddha himself.

Furthermore, regarding the subsequent reliance on the vehicles (*yāna*), there are differences among the various holy scriptures concerning their establishment of additions and subtractions, as well as the many differing explanations provided by ancient masters.
Some say that the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is as taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other such texts; thus, the *Pūrva-yoga-sūtra* states:
"Within the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, there is only the Dharma of the One Vehicle; there is neither a second nor a third.

While this principle appears throughout all Mahāyāna sūtras, scholars have traditionally transmitted two interpretations of its meaning. The first says: "The various vehicles were taught by the Buddha through skillful means (*upāya*), yet ultimately they all..."
Returning to the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, the other vehicles are merely the skillful means (*upāya*) of the One Vehicle;

therefore, it is taught that the two vehicles are themselves the Buddha-vehicle, for there are no two vehicles that can be called ultimate. As the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "The vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas all enter the Mahāyāna;
the Mahāyāna is itself the Buddha-vehicle. Thus, the three vehicles are identical to the One Vehicle, and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "In other lands I have become a Buddha under different names;
although these people harbor the notion that they have attained extinction and entered *nirvāṇa*, they shall seek the Buddha’s wisdom in those lands and hear this sutra.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There are pure and wondrous lands that transcend the three realms, where all *arhats* shall be born."

Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Good son, the dwelling place of a minor king is called a 'small city,' while the dwelling place of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) is called a 'great city.

The dwellings of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—whether eighty thousand, sixty thousand, forty thousand, twenty thousand, or ten thousand—are called nirvāṇa, but they are not the Great Nirvāṇa; they are not the unsurpassed Dharma King, the Holy King."
This dwelling place is named the Great Parinirvāṇa, Chapter Eleven. Furthermore, it says:
"The person who has attained the stage of Srotāpanna returns among humans and devas seven times, forever exhausting all suffering and entering Nirvāṇa;
such a person shall, after eighty thousand kalpas have passed, attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Even for a Pratyekabuddha, when afflictions are exhausted without remainder, they enter Nirvāṇa."
P’an (Bhānu) will, after ten thousand kalpas have passed, surely attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

From this we know that there are no two vehicles whose own fruits are ultimate or whose extinction is final. If even those of the two vehicles are thus, how could there be a class of people without the seed-nature who are called followers of the Human and Celestial Vehicles?
These are merely those of dull faculties who are not yet capable of entering the state of holiness; for their sake, the Buddha [established these paths].

To speak of shallow and mundane practices that cause one to leave the evil paths and be reborn among humans or devas—namely, the five precepts and so forth—is called the Vehicle of Humans and Devas (*manuṣyadevayāna*).
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "All sentient beings possess the mind [of awakening], and all shall achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Second, in reality, it is not that the distinctions between the five vehicles do not exist; rather, each attains the ultimate realization of the fruit within its own respective vehicle.
The various holy teachings state that there is but a single Buddha-vehicle (*ekayāna*) with reference to a specific intention, for it is not the case that there is truly only one.

Thus, the tenth volume of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "In order to attract and gather a certain class of beings and to sustain the remainder—those of indeterminate lineage—the Buddhas teach the Dharma of the Single Vehicle, such as selflessness and liberation; because their dispositions differ, they manifest through two intentions."
The ultimate teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is explained in detail in that treatise through ten reasons why the Buddha taught the Dharma of the One Vehicle.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra* states that there are four types of śrāvakas: first, those characterized by tranquility; second, those who have turned their minds toward bodhi—also called those who have regressed from bodhi;
third, those who are emanations (*nirmāṇa*); and fourth, those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*). The World-Honored One [taught] only for the sake of the second type.

Regarding the three bestowals of the prophecy of bodhi, were it otherwise, one would contradict the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra*, the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, and the *Mahāyāna-guṇavyūha-sūtra*;

one would also contradict the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the *Vyākhyāyukti*, the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra*. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "I..."
At one time, I taught that there is but one vehicle, one path, one practice, and one object;
I declared that from the stage of *srotāpanna* up to the *arhat*, all shall attain the Buddha-way. My disciples, failing to understand my intention, proclaimed these words among the great assembly:
"The Tathāgata has said that from the *srotāpanna* up to the *arhat*, all shall attain the Buddha-way; if they all become Buddhas..."

This refers to failing to understand the Buddha’s intent; because they do not understand the Buddha’s intent, they speak of "nature" (*svabhāva*) and "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) as they have been described here.

As extensively cited in the *Shengzhang* (Chapter on the Vehicle) regarding principle and scripture, there are those who, having heard various teachings, engage in arbitrary conceptualization, saying: "The sutra itself states that within the buddha-fields of the ten directions, there is only one [Buddha]."

Because there are neither two nor three vehicles of practice (*yāna*), one knows that the three vehicles are not the ultimate; by refuting the three, they are subsumed into the single ultimate vehicle.
Thus, the eighth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Among all the sentient beings in all worlds, those who desire to seek the path of the Śrāvaka are few;
those who seek the state of a Pratyekabuddha are even fewer; and those who seek the Mahāyāna are extremely rare."
To seek the Mahāyāna is still relatively easy; however, to be able to believe in this Dharma is extremely difficult to explain.

Because it is said that seeking the Mahāyāna is relatively easy while being able to believe in this Dharma is extremely difficult, we know that apart from the Mahāyāna, there is something difficult to believe in which is called the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Furthermore, [the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*] states in the twenty-ninth [chapter]: "If sentient beings are inferior and their minds are weary and submerged..."

He shows the path of the śrāvaka to lead them out of all sufferings; if there are sentient beings whose faculties are slightly clear and sharp who delight in the dharma of dependent origination, he speaks for them of the pratyekabuddha path;
if there are those with sharp faculties who benefit sentient beings and possess great compassion, he speaks for them of the bodhisattva path;
and if there are those with the unsurpassed mind who are determinedly delighted by the Great Matter, [he speaks of the Buddha path].

Because it is taught that the Buddha-vehicle (buddhayāna) reveals immeasurable Buddha-dharmas, and because it is stated that one who possesses great compassion teaches the path of the bodhisattva, we know that this is indeed the Mahāyāna within the three vehicles.

Furthermore, since it is said that those with the unsurpassed mind teach immeasurable Buddha-dharmas, we know that there is a separate One Vehicle (ekayāna) outside the three. This which has been established merely follows the teachings drawn forth according to their own nature.
This erroneous interpretation is not what was correctly stated. The meaning should be explained as "there is no second and no third.
This must mean that among the three vehicles, the Pratyekabuddha is the second and the Śrāvaka is the third.
It was spoken as a skillful means to attract those of indeterminate lineage and to sustain the rest; it does not mean that there truly are no two vehicles.
For what reason is the Mahāyāna said to be that which is to be refuted? Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "There is not even the Two Vehicles, let alone the Three.
Here, "two" refers to the second [vehicle] and "three" refers to the third; it is not that the Sūtra is generally stating that the two vehicles and the three vehicles are called "two" and "three.
Therefore, the Sūtra itself says: "This one reality alone is true; the other two are not real. It never uses the term "Lesser Vehicle" (hīnayāna).
If one delivers sentient beings by means of the three vehicles, yet there is something outside the three, why speak only of the other two as not being true?
It should also be said that the Lesser Vehicle does not deliver them, and thus the other three are likewise not true.
Furthermore, it should be said that in the world there are no people who attain extinction through the three vehicles; only through the Single Buddha Vehicle do they attain extinction.
The ear is taught as "cessation" (nirodha), and thus three types of nirvāṇa are spoken of. Why, then, is it said that there are only two vehicles for the sake of cessation?

Since the sūtras state only that the other two are not real and do not use the Lesser Vehicle to save others, and since it is clearly stated that two vehicles are taught for the sake of cessation, we know for certain that the Mahāyāna is not what is being refuted.
Furthermore, while three were previously mentioned, now only one is spoken of; the number is no longer three.

Therefore, the refutation of the three [vehicles] does not constitute a general refutation; rather, it specifically reveals that there is yet another [vehicle], such as the "One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*), which is a relative designation.
Since the two forms—namely, "small" and "large"—are mutually dependent, if both "small" and "two" are absent, then "one" and "large" are likewise non-existent.

This is as commonly known by scholars regarding categories such as long and short: although the name "one large" may not exist, the practice and fruit of the "one large" are nonetheless present. Thus, it is the One Vehicle.
The practices of the Mahāyāna and so forth are not to be refuted.

If one says that the "Great" within the three [vehicles] is what is refuted, then this is like the ox-cart permitted within the burning house; once outside the gate, the cart is given in its entirety.
If one were to refute the first ox and give a different ox later, how would these two oxen differ? Furthermore, regarding the "Great" among the three...
This clearly demonstrates that since it speaks of sudden enlightenment, how could it cause those who have entered the One Vehicle to become practitioners of gradual enlightenment?

Furthermore, what difference is there between the Mahāyāna and the One Vehicle regarding the arousal of the mind, the practice of cultivation, and the attainment of the fruit, such that one would abandon the Mahāyāna to separately adopt the One Vehicle?
The Lotus Sūtra states that for bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, the net of doubts has already been removed.
This reveals that those whose great resolve was about to regress before hearing the sutra now possess a firm and steadfast great mind after having heard it;

this is not like those who previously studied the Mahāyāna and now seek only the One Vehicle. There are two kinds of regression from the bodhicitta: first, those who have already regressed, such as Śāriputra and others;
second, those who are about to regress, such as these newly resolved ones, who, through hearing the sutra, have their previously cultivated and awakened resolve reinforced.

Regarding those whose subsequent resolve is firm and steadfast, the *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sūtra) states that the regression of the bodhicitta should be understood as either being about to regress or having already regressed,

based on the preceding principles and teachings. Furthermore, the claim that there exists a distinct One Vehicle (Ekayāna) outside of the three vehicles established by them is merely a product of deluded sentiment and lacks any basis whatsoever.

If it is said that seeking the Mahāyāna as taught in the *Avataṃsaka* is still relatively easy to do, yet believing in this Dharma is extremely difficult, this reveals that there is a distinct One Vehicle (Ekayāna) outside the three vehicles, which is called the ultimate vehicle and is thus termed "difficult to believe. Furthermore, the subsequent passage states:

"How much more so [is it difficult] to receive and uphold it, to correctly recollect it, to practice according to the teaching, and to understand it truly"—this indicates that even such [faith and practice] are still considered difficult to achieve.
It is easier to accept and uphold [the teachings], yet it is even more difficult than that; thus, one must establish a fifth vehicle as distinct [from the others].

However, although those sutras address seekers of the Mahāyāna who have already generated the great bodhicitta and have transcended the two vehicles—stating that this is "extremely rare"—they state that those who believe in this Dharma are even more difficult to find than those who merely generate the initial resolve, implying that hearing the Mahāyāna without slandering it is exceedingly difficult.
Next, one receives and maintains the Dharma that is even more difficult to believe; next, one practices that which is even more difficult to receive and maintain;

finally, there is the realization of reality, followed by further practice and so forth. As these stages progress, each subsequent level is superior to the preceding one. This does not imply a fault in the Dharma of faith;

rather, immediately upon the initial arousal of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), one establishes distinct vehicles (*yāna*) based on what is believed. Otherwise, if [the vehicles were not established], since the practice of receiving and maintaining would already surpass the Dharma of faith, one would then practice the realization of reality.

Successively surpassing the former, all such cases should be established as distinct vehicles (*yāna*). In that text, there are five points: first, manifesting the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*);
second, manifesting the arising of faith; third, manifesting the upholding [of the teachings]; fourth, practicing according to the instructions; and fifth, being able to realize [the goal].

That is to say, because of the bodhisattva practices, while shallow and deep faith and so forth are difficult to generate, the generation of the mind and so forth are easy. Since what is difficult later is not the same as what was difficult before, they are established as distinct vehicles.

If it were not so, then since the practices such as giving (*dāna*) of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are each progressively superior to those preceding them, one would have to establish separate vehicles (*yāna*) for each.
Furthermore, because the bodhicitta that initiates them, their causal practices, and the distinct fruits they attain differ from others, one might argue for establishing separate vehicles.

However, since the principle that all Bodhisattvas give rise to the mind of twofold benefit, practice the deeds of twofold benefit, and attain the fruits of twofold benefit is identical, they should not be established separately. Yet, [the Sūtra] says only...
Because vehicles are established according to the distinctions of practice, there is no fault even if there are many vehicles following those practices. As the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*, chapter sixty, states:
"In some worlds, one hears the name of a single vehicle; in others, two, three, four, five, or even an infinite number of vehicles.
While there are differences in the practice of wisdom, there is no difference in liberation."

If it is claimed that entering the Great Stage by a circuitous route is called the Mahāyāna, while proceeding directly is called the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) because of the greatness of the stage traversed, this too is irrational.
"Great" refers to vast wisdom; "One" excludes other teachings. It is not that the essential nature of the One is indeterminate.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that there is only the One Vehicle; it was originally intended for those of the Two Vehicles—how could it be [the One Vehicle] simply by virtue of proceeding directly?

Since the meaning of the name has not yet been fully understood, where could it possibly reside? Thus, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "The vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas all enter the Mahāyāna;
the Mahāyāna is precisely the Buddha-vehicle. From this perspective, the three vehicles are identical to the one vehicle.

Furthermore, regarding the twenty-nine passages cited by him, if one infers their underlying intent, they do not yet serve as proof. The meaning of that sūtra is intended to say: if there is compassion...
For those whose minds desire to benefit sentient beings, one preaches the Bodhisattva path in order to increase their compassion;

the Bodhisattva path consists of the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and so forth. For those who possess the unsurpassed mind and resolutely seek to become Buddhas, one preaches the merits of the Buddha in order to increase their joyful aspiration;
the merits of the Buddha consist of the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth.
The former is for the purpose of increasing the resolve to rescue sentient beings, while the latter is for the purpose of increasing the aspiration to seek Bodhi;

how could there be a separate teaching of a "One Vehicle" (Ekayāna) apart from these? From this, one should know that the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* teaches the One Vehicle with the intention of attracting one class of beings and sustaining the remainder;
since even the intentional teaching of a single vehicle is not ultimately real, how could there be two vehicles at all?

Is the Buddha-vehicle not the ultimate? Therefore, at the end of the twenty-seventh [chapter] and in the second stage (*bhūmi*) of the *Avataṃsaka*, all bodhisattvas are exhorted to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action.
Why is this? It is because by practicing these ten paths of wholesome action in conjunction with wisdom, one [attains the goal];
whereas if one is necessarily weak, delights in meager merit, feels weary of and fears the triple world, and possesses little great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one [must rely] on others.

If one hears the Dharma up to the level of the Śrāvaka-yāna and practices these ten paths of wholesome action, one will spontaneously attain wisdom without hearing it from another, becoming fully endowed with it and able to enter into the various causes and conditions of dharmas; this constitutes the Pratyekabuddha-yāna.
If one practices these ten paths of wholesome action with complete purity, and one’s mind becomes vast, immeasurable, and boundless, giving rise to great [compassion] among sentient beings...
One who possesses compassion and the power of skillful means, whose resolve is firm and who does not abandon any sentient being, seeks the singular wisdom of a Buddha;

by purifying the various stages (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva and the various *pāramitās*, and entering into profound and vast practices, one is then able to attain the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*),
the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and even the full realization of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).

The phrase "gathering all Buddha-dharmas" here demonstrates that the three vehicles (triyāna) are fully attained through the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*). If there were a separate [vehicle], why would it not be mentioned?

Could it be that those [beings] do not attain [the goal] by means of the ten paths of wholesome action? Indeed, in the second chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the "Fire House" chapter, it is taught that sentient beings have different faculties for the three vehicles;
likewise, in the first chapter of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, it is taught that those to be converted (*vineya*) are diverse. These two texts share the same meaning. *Yìyán* (義嚴).
I cannot cite extensively here, yet those who made such claims were unaware of their own errors; they subsequently altered the Buddhist scriptures according to their own ignorant whims.

Whether it be the sixty fascicles of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, or the tenth, twenty-eighth, and sixtieth [fascicles], as well as the first fascicle of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*—in these four locations, there are passages that have been modified. Those who examine them should search for these changes with great care.
I have revised the scriptural text and cannot describe it in full detail; rather, I have compared and examined it extensively against the old versions.

Apart from the three external vehicles, there is no one-vehicle (ekayāna) that is not directly identical to the practice of the Mahāyāna; thus, even the subtle distinctions of the three stages are not separate.
There are those who interpret the "extraordinary nature of the one great practice" based on the aforementioned meaning;

they extensively discuss the distinctions between the three stages and the differences in their respective practices, thereby manifesting how the one great practice differs from these stages. Furthermore, they speak of the differences between the three vehicles using a single term.

Although such texts exist that appear similar [to our own], when examined according to our own doctrine, they mostly do not accord with the intended meaning of those texts. How could we rely upon them to abruptly present the standard conventional view?

Not following the words of the Sage, various false explanations are refuted one by one as detailed in the separate excerpts. Up to this point, it has been taught exclusively that there is only the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Some speak of two vehicles: first, the Bodhisattva Vehicle, and second, the Śrāvaka Vehicle. The reasons for speaking of these two are the same as those previously mentioned regarding the two Piṭakas.

This is also called the "Two Vehicles" of the Great and Small: because the faculties, practices, and fruits of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are neither extensive nor equal, but rather narrow and inferior, they are collectively termed the "Hīnayāna. Because the faculties, practices, and fruits attained by Bodhisattvas are all vast and extensive, it is called the "Mahāyāna.
Alternatively, it is said that the three vehicles are the same; this is as explained in the *Samantaprabhā-sūtra* regarding the intent of the Tripiṭaka.
Those of indeterminate nature are not separately established because their ultimate attainment is also subsumed within the three vehicles alone, as the fruits obtained do not transcend these three.

Furthermore, the vehicles of humans and devas are not separately mentioned because they are equally shallow and proximate, being non-ultimate conveyances of tainted (*sāsrava*) fruits that are not to be desired.
Some say there are four vehicles, asserting that the indeterminate is separately established among the three vehicles.

Because they turn according to conditions and their fruits are not fixed, as is extensively taught in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and as the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* also states regarding the four vehicles—excluding those of indeterminate nature from the first four—the fruits attained do not exceed three;

since humans and devas are counted as one, there are thus four types. Among those without the lineage (*agotra*), because they are of a particularly superior birth, their conduct is capable of extensively carrying away evil.
The reason why humans and devas are combined [within the five vehicles] is that their faculties, practices, and fruits are equally shallow and mundane.
Some say that because the natures of the five vehicles—both determinate and indeterminate—are explained separately as four, and then humans and devas are combined, they are collectively termed "five.

This is as stated in the *Mahāyānaguṇasaṃvarṇana-sūtra* and the eighth fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts also explain the five vehicles separately.

Having already explained humans and devas as two, because there are distinctions among the classes of those who receive the retribution of their fruits, the indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*) is combined [with them] as it does not exceed these three.
Why is it that the existence of lineage (*gotra-sattva*) is not opened up to make four, and the absence of lineage (*agotra*) is not made two, such that six vehicles are taught?
This is because all the various teachings speak of five lineages; even if one were to speak of six, there would be no contradiction in meaning, yet we have not seen such a textual passage.
It speaks only of five and not seven, as there are no distinct categories [beyond them]; thus, the meaning of the increase and decrease is briefly clarified as in the chapter.
If one examines the basis [of this teaching], this treatise is subsumed under the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), for it teaches that the two vehicles are not ultimate;

within those two vehicles, they are gathered into the Bodhisattva Vehicle. Thus, both the four vehicles and the five vehicles are all the First [Vehicle]. This was previously discussed in the eighth [section].
This is the analysis of the basis.
○ Ninth, the analysis of how the teaching receives its name is as explained in the separate commentary.
○ Tenth, the judgment and explanation of the textual meaning should be understood from the text itself.

The above has primarily relied upon the oral transmissions of various masters; should there be slight differences in meaning or points worthy of contemplation and examination, let those who encounter them investigate their underlying intent in detail.
*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), Section on Discrimination, Part II (End).
